prompt: A growing sum of positive terms is claimed to stay below two. The hypothesis “below two” alone does not leave a known amount of space for the next term. Why can proving a stronger bound with a specified remaining gap help?

options.text: Stronger claims always have easier base cases
options.explanation: The stronger claim can make the base harder. Its benefit here is the extra information available in the step.

options.text: It records enough remaining space to absorb the next term
options.explanation: Correct. A specified gap can be compared with the next addition, unlike the bare statement “below two”.

options.text: The bound must be the exact sum
options.explanation: A bound can leave slack. Its usefulness for induction does not make it an equality.

options.text: It automatically changes ordinary induction into strong induction
options.explanation: The step can still use only the immediately preceding case. Strengthening changes the claim, not which earlier cases are available.

workedExample: “Below two” gives no usable estimate of the remaining space. The stronger bound supplies a guaranteed gap that can pay for the next positive term. The proof must establish that tighter bound at the base and preserve it at each step. It remains ordinary induction because it uses only the preceding case.

prompt: A merge-sort-style cost model says one item costs one step. A proposed exact formula counts merging work but predicts zero work at one item. What should a proof reviewer conclude?

options.text: The formula is established if it matches a large input
options.explanation: One matching example cannot establish the general formula.

options.text: The base case can be skipped because recursion handles it
options.explanation: The base case starts the recursion proof and must match the model.

options.text: The formula must be right asymptotically, so it is right exactly
options.explanation: An asymptotic bound and an exact cost are different claims.

options.text: The exact formula fails its base case and needs revision
options.explanation: Correct. The model charges leaf work that this formula omitted.

workedExample: A proof must cover the smallest allowed size before invoking the recurrence. Ignoring the work at the leaves can yield a formula that looks plausible for merging but already fails at one item. The recursive step then needs a claim that includes both smaller-call costs and current merging work.
